lessons.title: What time is it? Uhr and um
lessons.goal: Tell the official time and say at what time something starts.

grammar.point: Official time says hour + Uhr + minutes (14:30 = vierzehn Uhr dreißig). um + time says at that time; the verb stays in part 2.
grammar.oneLine: Es ist acht Uhr. Der Film beginnt um 20 Uhr. Um 20 Uhr beginnt der Film.

mistake.why: You need um in front of a clock time.

terms.meaning: o'clock: stuck on the hour number and it never changes
the 24-hour clock used for timetables
the word for at in front of a clock time
the number after Uhr in official time

cards.title: Before we start: telling the time
cards.body: Your film starts soon and a friend asks: "When?" This chapter is about everyday life: time, family, my and your, can and must, and making appointments. Today is the clock. You already put a time first and kept the verb in place 2. Now the time gets a real clock.
steps: You already know: a time can start the sentence and the verb stays in part 2 (am Montag, chapter 2)
New today: Uhr and um, to say the time and at what time something starts
By the end you can: ask Wie spät ist es? and say when a film or a course begins

examples.de: Um neun Uhr beginnt der Kurs.
examples.en: At nine o'clock the course starts.
examples.why: New today: um + a clock time. The verb is still part 2.

cards.more: Think of a clock as a street sign. In chapter 2 you learned the sign for days: am Montag. Now you learn the sign for clock times: um. The sentence itself does not change at all. The verb sits in chair 2, like always. Only the little time label is new. German trains and cinemas use the 24-hour clock, so after 12 the numbers just keep going. You will meet this step by step in the next cards: first how to ask, then the 24-hour clock, then um.

cards.title: Ask and tell the time: Uhr
cards.body: Ask: Wie spät ist es? (How late is it?) Answer: Es ist + number + Uhr. Uhr means o'clock and never changes. One o'clock is ein Uhr, with ein, not eins.

examples.why: Say ein Uhr, not eins Uhr.

cards.more: Think of Uhr as a little label stuck on the number, like o'clock in English. You say the number, then stick on Uhr. Step 1: Es ist. Step 2: the number, for example zehn. Step 3: Uhr. Es ist zehn Uhr. The label never gets a plural or an ending. Extra example: Es ist zwölf Uhr.

cards.title: Official time: the 24-hour clock
cards.body: On trains, at the cinema and on the radio, Germans use the 24-hour clock. Say the hour, Uhr, then the minutes as a normal number. 14:30 is vierzehn Uhr dreißig.
cards.more: A train timetable must be clear, so it uses one single way to say every time. No halves, no quarters. It is just two numbers with Uhr between them. Step 1: say the hour. Step 2: say Uhr. Step 3: say the minutes. Nothing at all after the minutes. 20:05 is zwanzig Uhr fünf. Extra example: 9:40 is neun Uhr vierzig.

cards.title: After 12: subtract 12
cards.body: The 24-hour clock goes on after 12. For a clock with 12 hours, subtract 12. 15 Uhr is 3 in the afternoon. 20 Uhr is 8 in the evening. Early times (0 to 12) stay the same.

examples.de: Der Zug fährt um fünfzehn Uhr.
Das Kino beginnt um zwanzig Uhr.

cards.more: Imagine the day as two laps round a clock face. The second lap starts at 13. To find the small number, take away 12. Step 1: is the number bigger than 12? Step 2: subtract 12. Step 3: that is the time on a normal clock. 17 Uhr: 17 minus 12 is 5. So 5 in the afternoon. Extra example: 22 Uhr is 10 at night.

cards.title: um: at what time?
cards.body: um means at when you give a clock time. Wann beginnt der Film? (When does the film start?) The film starts at 20:00: Der Film beginnt um 20 Uhr. The verb is still part 2.

examples.de: Der Film beginnt um zwanzig Uhr.
Der Zug fährt um vierzehn Uhr dreißig.

cards.more: In English you say at 8 o'clock. German uses a little word for at: um. It goes right in front of the time. Step 1: say your sentence: Der Kurs beginnt. Step 2: add um. Step 3: add the time: um neun Uhr. Never leave um out. Extra example: Der Bus fährt um sieben Uhr.

cards.title: Start with the time: the verb stays second
cards.body: The time can go to the start of the sentence. The verb stays in part 2. The subject then moves behind the verb. Um neun Uhr beginnt der Kurs.

examples.de: Um neun Uhr beginnt der Kurs.
examples.why: Part 1 = the time, part 2 = the verb.

examples.de: Um vierzehn Uhr dreißig fährt der Zug.
examples.why: The subject comes after the verb.

examples.de: Um zwanzig Uhr beginnt das Kino.

cards.more: You know this from chapter 2: am Montag spiele ich Tennis. The time can lead, but the verb never gives up its second chair. Step 1: count the parts. Step 2: the time is one part, so it fills chair 1. Step 3: the verb takes chair 2. Step 4: the subject takes chair 3. Extra example: Um sieben Uhr frühstücke ich.

cards.title: Start, end, last: beginnen, enden, dauern
cards.body: Three verbs for time: beginnen (to start), enden (to end), dauern (to last). All are regular. enden adds an extra e: er endet. For how long, say the number and Stunden: Der Kurs dauert zwei Stunden.

examples.de: Der Film beginnt um zwanzig Uhr.
Der Film endet um zweiundzwanzig Uhr.
examples.why: enden: stem ends in d, so er endet.

rows: Der Kurs beginnt um neun Uhr.
Der Kurs endet um zwölf Uhr.

cards.more: Every event has three questions. When does it start? When does it end? How long does it last? Step 1: beginnen answers the first one. Step 2: enden answers the second. Step 3: dauern answers the third, and no um is needed, because it is not a clock time. Remember the extra e from chapter 2: er endet. Extra example: Der Kurs dauert eine Stunde.

lessons.title: Everyday time: halb, Viertel, nach and vor
lessons.goal: Say the time the way friends say it, and understand halb.

grammar.point: Everyday time uses nach, vor, Viertel and halb. halb names the next hour: halb drei = 2:30.
grammar.oneLine: Es ist halb drei. Es ist Viertel nach drei. Es ist kurz vor acht.

mistake.why: halb names the next hour, not the hour you see.

terms.meaning: the short way to say the time with friends: halb, Viertel, nach, vor
a quarter: 15 minutes
half way to the hour you say
after / before

cards.title: Before we start: the everyday clock
cards.body: A friend texts: "We meet at half past two." Last lesson you learned the official time for trains. Friends use a shorter way. It has a famous trap: halb. Today you learn to read it without panic.
steps: You already know: Es ist vierzehn Uhr dreißig, the official time from the last lesson
New today: nach, vor, Viertel and halb, the everyday way to say the time
By the end you can: say and understand Es ist halb drei and Viertel nach drei

examples.de: Der Kurs beginnt um neun Uhr.
examples.en: The course starts at nine o'clock.

examples.de: Der Kurs beginnt um halb neun.
examples.en: The course starts at half past eight.
examples.why: New today: halb neun means 8:30, half way to nine.

cards.more: Imagine a hill with the hour at the top. Everyday time says how far you have climbed. Nach means you just left the hour, vor means the next hour is nearly there. Viertel is a quarter of the way. Halb is the tricky one: you are half way to the next hour, so halb neun is 8:30, not 9:30. German always names the hour you are walking towards. It feels odd for a day or two, and then it clicks. The next cards go one piece at a time.

cards.title: Everyday time: nach and vor
cards.body: Friends say the time in a shorter way. nach means after and vor means before. fünf nach drei is 3:05. zehn vor drei is 2:50. In everyday time you can leave out Uhr.
cards.more: English does the same: five past three, ten to three. Look at the clock face. The minute hand has passed the hour: use nach. The minute hand has not reached the next hour yet: use vor. Step 1: say the minutes. Step 2: choose nach or vor. Step 3: say the hour you are near. Extra example: zwanzig nach acht is 8:20.

cards.title: Viertel nach and Viertel vor
cards.body: Viertel means quarter. A quarter past is Viertel nach: 3:15 is Viertel nach drei. A quarter to is Viertel vor: 2:45 is Viertel vor drei. There is no number for the minutes here.

examples.en: It is a quarter past three (3:15).
It is a quarter to three (2:45).
It is a quarter to eight (7:45).

steps: 3:15 → Viertel nach drei
2:45 → Viertel vor drei
7:15 → Viertel nach sieben
7:45 → Viertel vor acht
cards.more: A pizza cut in four: one slice is a Viertel, a quarter. A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes. So Viertel nach is fifteen minutes after, and Viertel vor is fifteen minutes before. Step 1: 15 minutes past the hour? Viertel nach. Step 2: 15 minutes before the next hour? Viertel vor. Step 3: add the hour. Extra example: Viertel nach neun is 9:15.

cards.title: halb: half way to the next hour
cards.body: Careful! halb drei is not 3:30. halb drei is 2:30. halb means half way to the hour that you say. Always name the next hour. 8:30 is halb neun.

examples.why: halb drei = half way to three.
halb acht = half way to eight.
halb zwölf = half way to twelve.

cards.more: English says half past two: you look back at two. German looks forward: half way to three. That is why German says halb drei for 2:30. Step 1: it is 2:30. Step 2: which hour comes next? Three. Step 3: say halb and that hour: halb drei. Always add one to the hour you see. Extra example: 6:30 is halb sieben.

cards.title: kurz nach, kurz vor, genau
cards.body: Nobody says the exact minute all day. kurz nach means just after. kurz vor means just before. genau means exactly. Use them with an hour or a half hour.

examples.why: kurz nach = a few minutes after.
kurz vor = a few minutes before.

examples.en: It is exactly half past nine.

cards.more: Imagine a friend asks the time. You glance at the clock: 3:02. You do not say drei Uhr zwei. You say kurz nach drei, just after three. Step 1: look at the clock. Step 2: is it a few minutes past or before? Step 3: say kurz nach or kurz vor and the hour. If it is perfect, say genau. Extra example: Es ist genau zwölf Uhr.

cards.title: Two ways to say the same time
cards.body: Use official time for timetables, trains and appointments with an office. Use everyday time with friends and family. Both are right. Learn to understand both.

examples.de: Der Zug fährt um vierzehn Uhr dreißig.

examples.en: We meet Mira at half past two. (friends)

examples.de: Das Kino beginnt um Viertel vor acht.
examples.en: The cinema starts at a quarter to eight.

cards.more: It is like a formal and a casual way of speaking. A bus driver on the loudspeaker is formal. Your friend at the door is casual. Step 1: timetable or office? Use hour + Uhr + minutes. Step 2: friends or family? Use halb, Viertel, nach and vor. Step 3: after 12 Uhr, official time uses 13 to 24, everyday uses 1 to 12. Extra example: 18:15 is also Viertel nach sechs.

cards.title: um + everyday time
cards.body: um works with everyday time too. Um halb drei means at half past two. Um Viertel nach acht means at a quarter past eight. The verb is still part 2.

examples.de: Der Kurs beginnt um halb neun.
examples.en: The course starts at half past eight.

examples.de: Um Viertel vor acht frühstücke ich.
examples.en: At a quarter to eight I have breakfast.
examples.why: Time first: the verb is still second.

cards.more: um is the little at word. You use it in front of any clock time, official or everyday. Step 1: write the sentence: Der Kurs beginnt. Step 2: add um. Step 3: add the everyday time: halb neun. If the time goes first, the verb stays second, and the subject comes after it. Extra example: Um halb sieben esse ich.

lessons.title: When it starts, ends and lasts: am, um, von … bis
lessons.goal: Say when something is open or happens, and for how long.

grammar.point: um + clock time, am + day or part of the day, von … bis for a time span. The verb stays in part 2.
grammar.oneLine: Am Montag arbeite ich von acht bis sechzehn Uhr. Das Café ist am Sonntag geschlossen.

mistake.why: A clock time needs um, a day needs am.

terms.meaning: a small word that tells when or where, like um, am, von, bis
from one time to another time
the hours a shop or office is open

cards.title: Before we start: when it starts and ends
cards.body: A shop sign says: open from eight to six. A course runs from nine to twelve. Today you say a whole stretch of time. It joins two things you know: am for days and um for clock times.
steps: You already know: am for a day and um for a clock time
New today: von … bis, from one time to another
By the end you can: say when something is open or when you work

examples.de: Der Kurs beginnt um acht Uhr.
examples.en: The course starts at eight o'clock.

examples.de: Das Café ist von acht bis achtzehn Uhr offen.
examples.en: The café is open from eight to six.
examples.why: New today: von … bis puts a start and an end round the times.

cards.more: Think of a bridge. Von is where you step onto it and bis is where you step off. Everything between is the time something lasts. Uhr only goes once, at the end, like a stamp on the bridge ticket. The rest is what you know: the verb is in chair 2, and a day can lead the sentence. You will also learn the parts of the day and the words offen and geschlossen. One small step at a time in the next cards.

cards.title: um or am?
cards.body: You know am from the days: am Montag. um is for clock times: um acht Uhr. Look at what you say: a day gets am, a clock time gets um.

examples.de: Der Kurs beginnt um acht Uhr.
Am Montag beginnt der Kurs um acht Uhr.
examples.en: On Monday the course starts at eight.
examples.why: am + day, um + time, in one sentence.

cards.more: Think of two shelves. The shelf for days has the label am. The shelf for clock times has the label um. Step 1: what is the time word? Step 2: Monday, Tuesday, Sunday: shelf am. Step 3: eight o'clock, half past two: shelf um. You can use both in one sentence. Extra example: Am Freitag beginnt der Film um zwanzig Uhr.

cards.title: Parts of the day
cards.body: Six parts of the day: der Morgen, der Vormittag, der Mittag, der Nachmittag, der Abend. For these, use am: am Morgen. For night, learn in der Nacht as one piece.

examples.en: In the morning I drink coffee.
In the afternoon I learn German.

examples.why: a chunk: learn in der Nacht as one piece.

cards.more: Your day has slices, like a cake. Morning, then late morning, then noon, then afternoon, then evening. Every slice gets am. Night is the odd one: in der Nacht. Why der? That comes later. Learn it as one piece. Step 1: pick the slice. Step 2: put am in front. Step 3: the verb stays second. Extra example: Am Abend koche ich.

cards.title: von … bis: from … to
cards.body: von means from and bis means until. Put them round the two times: von neun bis zwölf Uhr. You say Uhr once, after the second time. This answers: for how long, from when to when?

examples.de: Der Kurs ist von neun bis zwölf Uhr.
examples.en: The course is from nine to twelve.

examples.de: Ich arbeite von acht bis sechzehn Uhr.
examples.en: I work from eight to sixteen.

examples.de: Der Film ist von zwanzig Uhr bis zweiundzwanzig Uhr.
examples.why: You may say Uhr twice too.

cards.more: A bridge needs two ends. von is the start end, bis is the finish end. Step 1: say the start time. Step 2: put von in front of it. Step 3: say the end time with bis in front. Step 4: finish with Uhr. You can also use von … bis with days: von Montag bis Freitag. Extra example: Ich lerne von zehn bis zwölf Uhr.

cards.title: Day + time + von … bis: the word order
cards.body: You can put the day first. The verb stays in part 2. Then the subject, then von … bis. Am Montag arbeite ich von acht bis sechzehn Uhr. Or start with the subject: Ich arbeite am Montag von acht bis sechzehn Uhr.

cards.more: Imagine three chairs again. Chair 2 is always for the verb. Chair 1 and the rest can be swapped. Step 1: put the verb in chair 2. Step 2: choose what sits in chair 1: the day, or ich. Step 3: add everything else after. The meaning stays the same, only the focus changes. Extra example: Am Dienstag koche ich von sechs bis sieben Uhr.

cards.title: Ask: Wie lange? Von wann bis wann?
cards.body: Wie lange? asks for how long. Von wann bis wann? asks for the start and the end. Answer with von … bis or with dauern.

examples.de: Von wann bis wann ist der Kurs?
examples.en: From when to when is the course?

rows: Von wann bis wann ist der Kurs?

cards.more: Three useful questions. When: Wann? A moment in time. How long: Wie lange? A length of time. From when to when: Von wann bis wann? Start and end. Step 1: pick the question that fits what you want to know. Step 2: the verb is part 2, always. Step 3: answer with um, von … bis or a number of Stunden. Extra example: Wann beginnt der Kurs? Um acht Uhr.

cards.title: Opening hours: offen and geschlossen
cards.body: Shops have Öffnungszeiten (opening hours). offen means open and geschlossen means closed. After sein, they have no ending. Das Café ist von acht bis achtzehn Uhr offen.

examples.en: The café is open from eight to eighteen.

examples.en: On Sunday the bank is closed.

examples.en: The supermarket is open on Saturday.

steps: Das Café ist offen.
Das Café ist von acht bis achtzehn Uhr offen.
Am Sonntag ist das Café geschlossen.
cards.more: A shop sign says Offen or Geschlossen. It is just sein + an adjective, like groß or schön in chapter 3. No ending. Step 1: pick the place. Step 2: sein: ist. Step 3: add the times. Step 4: end with offen or geschlossen. Extra example: Die Bank ist von neun bis sechzehn Uhr offen.

cards.title: Home and work: nach Hause, zu Hause
cards.body: nach Hause means home (going home). zu Hause means at home. Learn both as one piece each. Why is it Hause? That comes later. Ich gehe um siebzehn Uhr nach Hause.

examples.de: Ich gehe um siebzehn Uhr nach Hause.
examples.en: I go home at seventeen hundred.

examples.de: Am Abend bin ich zu Hause.
examples.en: In the evening I am at home.

cards.more: Two small pieces to remember. nach Hause answers where to? You move. zu Hause answers where? You stay. Step 1: do you move? Use nach Hause with gehen or fahren. Step 2: do you stay? Use zu Hause with sein. Do not change the words for now. Extra example: Ich fahre um achtzehn Uhr nach Hause.

grammar.oneLine: Ich habe einen Bruder. Ich habe keine Schwester. Wie viele Geschwister hast du?

mistake.why: Bruder is masculine and it is the object: ein becomes einen.

a word that has no singular, like die Eltern
how many

cards.title: Before we start: my family
cards.body: Someone asks: "Do you have brothers and sisters?" You can already say what you have, like a dog or a coffee. Today the same sentence talks about people in your family.
steps: You already know: haben with an object, and masculine einen (chapter 4)
New today: family words, Vater, Mutter, Bruder, Schwester and more
By the end you can: say who is in your family and ask Hast du Geschwister?

examples.why: New today: the same sentence, a family word at the end.
New today: keine, as you learned with kein.

cards.more: A family is like a little team, and every player has a name tag with der, die or das. You already know how to say what you have. Swap the dog for a brother and the sentence works exactly the same. Only masculine words change, einen Bruder, but eine Schwester stays. There are also words for several people at once: die Eltern, die Geschwister. Learn each noun with its article. The next cards take it person by person.

cards.title: Parents: Vater, Mutter, Eltern
cards.body: der Vater is the father and die Mutter is the mother. Together they are die Eltern: the parents. Eltern only exists in the plural, so it uses die and sind.
cards.more: Family words are nouns like any others. Each one has a gender and a plural. Step 1: learn the article: der Vater, die Mutter. Step 2: learn that Eltern is always plural, like scissors in English. Step 3: for many things you say sind, not ist. Extra example: Die Eltern sind nett.

cards.title: Brother, sister, siblings
cards.body: der Bruder is the brother and die Schwester is the sister. The plural for both together is die Geschwister: brothers and sisters, siblings. Learn the plural of each word.
cards.more: German has a word for brothers and sisters together. English uses siblings, which is rare. German Geschwister is normal. Step 1: one boy: der Bruder. Step 2: one girl: die Schwester. Step 3: both together: die Geschwister. Step 4: haben takes an object, so Bruder is masculine and becomes einen. Extra example: Ich habe zwei Brüder.

cards.title: Son, daughter, child
cards.body: der Sohn is the son and die Tochter is the daughter. You already know das Kind (child). Parents and children make a family: die Familie.
cards.more: A family tree has three levels: parents, you and your siblings, and children. Step 1: son: der Sohn, plural die Söhne. Step 2: daughter: die Tochter, plural die Töchter. Step 3: child: das Kind, plural die Kinder. Step 4: remember the accusative rule from chapter 4: only the masculine takes einen. Extra example: Herr Ali hat zwei Kinder.

cards.title: Grandparents: Großvater, Großmutter
cards.body: der Großvater is the grandfather and die Großmutter is the grandmother. Together: die Großeltern. In the family you say Opa and Oma. They are short, friendly forms.
cards.more: You can build long German words from small ones. groß means big, and Vater means father. So Großvater is big father. Step 1: Großvater = groß + Vater. Step 2: Großmutter = groß + Mutter. Step 3: the last part gives the gender: der Vater, so der Großvater. In the family: Opa and Oma. Extra example: Oma kocht Suppe.

cards.title: Ich habe …: family and the accusative
cards.body: haben takes an object, so the accusative rule works: masculine einen, feminine eine, neuter ein. To say none: keinen, keine, kein. Plural: no article. keine Geschwister.

examples.en: I do not have a sister.

cards.more: This is the same rule you used for food in chapter 4. Only the masculine changes. Step 1: do you have it? Use ein-form: einen Bruder, eine Schwester, ein Kind. Step 2: do you not have it? Use kein-form: keinen Bruder, keine Schwester, kein Kind. Step 3: many of them? No article, or keine. Extra example: Ich habe zwei Kinder.

cards.title: Ask: Hast du Geschwister? Wie viele?
cards.body: Ask Hast du Geschwister? (yes/no, verb first). Ask Wie viele Geschwister hast du? for how many. wie viele means how many and is followed by a plural noun. Answer with a number.

examples.en: How many siblings do you have?

steps: Hast du Geschwister?
Ja, ich habe eine Schwester.
Wie viele Kinder hast du?
Ich habe zwei Kinder.
cards.more: The conversation has two steps. First a yes/no question to start. Then how many, to learn more. Step 1: Hast du Geschwister? Step 2: Ja, ich habe eine Schwester. Step 3: Wie viele Kinder hast du? Step 4: Ich habe zwei Kinder. The verb is always in chair 2 in a W-question. Extra example: Wie viele Brüder hast du?

cards.title: Tell about a person: er, sie
cards.body: After you name a person, use er (he) or sie (she). Er heißt Ben. Sie ist zwanzig Jahre alt. For jobs: Er arbeitet als Arzt. You know all of this from chapters 1 and 2.

examples.de: Ich habe einen Bruder. Er heißt Ben.
examples.en: I have a brother. He is called Ben.

examples.de: Ich habe eine Schwester. Sie ist zwanzig Jahre alt.

cards.more: In German, he, she and it follow the noun's gender. Step 1: look at the noun: Bruder is der, so er. Step 2: Schwester is die, so sie. Step 3: Kind is das, so es. Step 4: the verb ending follows: er heißt, sie ist, es ist. Extra example: Ich habe einen Sohn. Er ist fünf Jahre alt.

lessons.title: mein and dein: my and your
lessons.goal: Say whose family and things you mean, with mein and dein, as subject and as object.

grammar.point: mein and dein take the same endings as ein and kein. Accusative: only the masculine changes: mein → meinen, dein → deinen.
grammar.oneLine: Das ist mein Bruder. Ich treffe meinen Bruder. Wo ist deine Tasche?

mistake.why: Bruder is masculine and the object: mein becomes meinen.

terms.meaning: a word like mein or dein that shows who owns something
the person who has the thing
a word that takes the same endings as ein and kein: mein, dein, sein, ihr …

cards.title: Before we start: my and your
cards.body: Is that your phone? Yes, that is my phone. To talk about what belongs to people, you need little owner words. Good news: you already know how they end, because they act like ein and kein.
steps: You already know: ein and kein, only the masculine changes in the accusative (einen, keinen)
New today: mein and dein, with the very same endings
By the end you can: say Das ist mein Bruder and Ich treffe meinen Bruder

examples.why: New today: mein takes the endings of ein, so einen becomes meinen.
New today: mein, no ending, like ein.

cards.more: Think of ein as a coat and mein as the same coat with your name sewn in. The coat fits exactly the same way: nothing for der and das words, an extra e for die words and for many things, and en for a masculine object. So you do not learn new endings. You only learn two new little words, mein and dein. In the next cards you will see the table, the object form and how to choose the word and the ending in two small steps.

cards.title: mein and dein: my and your
cards.body: A possessive article shows who something belongs to. mein means my. dein means your (for a friend, du). It stands in front of a noun, like ein does. Das ist mein Bruder.
cards.more: Words like my and your show who owns something. In German they are tiny words in front of the noun, just like ein. mein belongs to ich, because ich = I, my. dein belongs to du, because du = you, your. Step 1: who owns it? Me: mein. You: dein. Step 2: put it before the noun. Extra example: Das ist mein Auto.

cards.title: Same endings as ein and kein
cards.body: mein and dein take the same endings as ein and kein. Masculine and neuter: nothing. Feminine: add -e. Plural: add -e. Compare the table.
cards.more: You already know this pattern from kein: kein Bruder, keine Schwester, kein Kind, keine Eltern. mein works the same way, because mein is also an ein-word. Step 1: find the noun's gender. Step 2: masculine or neuter: mein. Step 3: feminine or plural: meine. Step 4: for dein, change m to d. Extra example: Das ist deine Mutter.

cards.title: The accusative: meinen, deinen
cards.body: As an object, only the masculine changes. mein becomes meinen and dein becomes deinen. Feminine, neuter and plural stay the same. Ich treffe meinen Bruder. Ich sehe meine Schwester.
cards.more: Same rule as ein: only the masculine word gets -en when it is the object. Step 1: is the noun the object, the thing the verb acts on? Step 2: is it masculine? Add -en: meinen. Step 3: feminine, neuter, plural: nothing changes. Say it out loud: ein Bruder, einen Bruder, mein Bruder, meinen Bruder. Extra example: Ich habe deinen Stift.

cards.title: Plural: meine, deine
cards.body: Many things: meine and deine, in the nominative and the accusative. There is no change. Meine Eltern wohnen in Wien. Ich treffe meine Eltern.
steps: many things → meine, deine
subject: Meine Eltern wohnen in Wien.
object: Ich treffe meine Eltern.
same word, same form
cards.more: A plural noun always acts like a die-word. In the nominative and in the accusative the form is meine. Step 1: is the noun plural? Step 2: use meine or deine. Step 3: no extra ending, because nothing changes for the object. You will see Bücher: it is the plural of das Buch, with an umlaut and -er. Extra example: Meine Geschwister sind nett.

cards.title: Owner picks the word, noun picks the ending
cards.body: Two questions for every possessive. 1: who owns it? ich → mein, du → dein. 2: which noun, and is it a subject or an object? That gives the ending. Tell them apart.

examples.why: owner ich; Computer is masculine object.

cards.more: Think of a two-step lock. Lock one is the owner: me or you? That chooses the start: mein or dein. Lock two is the noun: its gender and its job in the sentence. That chooses the ending. The two locks do not talk to each other. Step 1: owner. Step 2: gender of the noun. Step 3: subject or object? Extra example: Ich lese dein Buch.

cards.title: Ask and answer with mein and dein
cards.body: Use dein to ask a friend. Use mein to answer. Ist das dein Handy? Ja, das ist mein Handy. Wie heißt dein Bruder? Mein Bruder heißt Ben.

examples.why: The subject can start with mein.

cards.more: In a chat, the other person says dein, and you answer with mein. It flips like a mirror. Step 1: question: Wie heißt dein Bruder? Step 2: answer: Mein Bruder heißt Ben. Step 3: yes/no question: Ist das dein Auto? Step 4: answer: Ja, das ist mein Auto. Nein, das ist nicht mein Auto. Extra example: Wo ist dein Stift?

drills.hint: Feminine object: no change from the nominative.

lessons.goal: Say his, her, our, your (all) and polite your, as subject and as object.

grammar.point: Every owner has a possessive: mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, ihr, Ihr. They take the ein-endings: -e for feminine and plural, -en for a masculine object.
grammar.oneLine: Das ist sein Bruder. Das ist ihre Schwester. Ich sehe unseren Hund.

mistake.wrong: Leon hat eine Schwester. Das ist ihre Schwester.
mistake.right: Leon hat eine Schwester. Das ist seine Schwester.
mistake.why: The owner decides: Leon is a he, so sein. The noun decides the -e.

terms.meaning: the person who has the thing
the start of the word: mein-, sein-, unser-
your (several friends): the middle e disappears before an ending

cards.title: Before we start: all the owner words
cards.body: Ben has a brother. Whose brother is that? His. Today you meet the rest of the owner words: his, her, our, your (two friends), their and polite your. They all use the endings you just learned.
steps: You already know: mein and dein with the ein-endings (the last lesson)
New today: sein, ihr, unser, euer and Ihr, with the same endings
By the end you can: say who something belongs to, for any owner

examples.why: New today: sein means his here, and the masculine object still ends in -en.
New today: unser, no ending, like ein.

cards.more: Imagine nine owners standing in a line: I, you, he, she, it, we, you two, they and polite you. Each one has its own word, from mein to Ihr. That is the only new part. The ending is the old friend you already know, the same as ein. One trap helps to remember: the owner picks the word, but the noun picks the ending. The next cards walk along the line one owner at a time.

cards.title: sein and ihr: his and her
cards.body: sein means his (and its). ihr means her. Look at the owner: a man or a boy gives sein. A woman or a girl gives ihr. Ben hat einen Bruder. Das ist sein Bruder.

examples.de: Ben hat einen Bruder. Das ist sein Bruder.
examples.en: Ben has a brother. That is his brother.

examples.de: Anna hat einen Bruder. Das ist ihr Bruder.
examples.en: Anna has a brother. That is her brother.

examples.de: Das ist Leon. Sein Vater heißt Paul.
examples.en: That is Leon. His father is called Paul.

cards.more: In the last lesson you learned mein for ich and dein for du. Now the same idea for he and she. Step 1: who owns it? A man: er, so sein. A woman: sie, so ihr. Step 2: put it before the noun, like ein. Step 3: the ending still follows the noun: sein Bruder, seine Schwester. Extra example: Anna hat eine Katze. Das ist ihre Katze.

cards.title: The trap: the owner picks the word
cards.body: The owner picks sein or ihr. The noun picks the ending. Leon has a sister: seine Schwester (Leon is a he, Schwester is feminine). Anna has a brother: ihr Bruder (Anna is a she, Bruder is masculine).

examples.de: Leon hat eine Schwester. Das ist seine Schwester.
examples.en: Leon has a sister. That is his sister.

examples.de: Anna hat einen Bruder. Das ist ihr Bruder.
examples.en: Anna has a brother. That is her brother.
examples.why: she → ihr, masculine noun → no ending.

examples.de: Anna hat eine Schwester. Das ist ihre Schwester.
examples.en: Anna has a sister. That is her sister.

cards.more: English only looks at the owner: his sister, her brother. German looks at two things. Step 1: the owner. He gives sein. She gives ihr. Step 2: the noun. Feminine or plural: add e. Masculine or neuter: nothing. So a man with a sister says seine Schwester. His is male, but Schwester is female, and the e comes from Schwester. Extra example: Leon hat einen Hund. Das ist sein Hund.

cards.title: wir → unser
cards.body: unser means our. The owner is wir. unser takes the ein-endings: unser Vater, unsere Mutter, unser Kind, unsere Eltern. Wir haben einen Sohn. Das ist unser Sohn.
cards.more: unser is the possessive for we. It is a longer word, but the endings are easy because they work like mein. Step 1: owner wir, so unser. Step 2: add the ending for the noun. Masculine and neuter: nothing. Feminine and plural: -e. Step 3: for the masculine object: unseren. Extra example: Wir besuchen unseren Onkel.

cards.title: ihr → euer (a special one)
cards.body: euer means your, when you talk to two or more friends (ihr). It loses its second e when it gets an ending: euer Vater, but eure Mutter, euren Vater. Say it out loud.
cards.more: euer is the lazy one. It drops the middle e so that it is easier to say. Step 1: no ending: euer Vater. Step 2: with an ending, throw out the middle e: eure Mutter. Step 3: object masculine: euren. Do not say euere or eueren. Extra example: Ist das euer Hund?

cards.title: ihr (they) and Ihr (polite)
cards.body: Two more owners. sie (they) gives ihr: die Kinder und ihre Eltern. Sie (polite you) gives Ihr with a capital I: Wie heißt Ihre Frau? Context shows which one it is. Capital letter = polite.

examples.de: Die Kinder und ihre Eltern wohnen in Wien.
examples.en: The children and their parents live in Vienna.

examples.de: Frau Weber, wie heißt Ihr Sohn?
examples.en: Frau Weber, what is your son called?

examples.de: Herr Ali, ist das Ihr Auto?
examples.en: Herr Ali, is that your car?

cards.more: ihr has three jobs in total, like sie. She, they: ihr. Polite you: Ihr with a capital letter, like Sie. Step 1: who owns it? One woman or girl: ihr. Many people: ihr. A stranger or Frau Weber: Ihr. Step 2: add the noun's ending as usual. Step 3: at the start of a sentence, you cannot see the capital. Use the situation. Extra example: Ihre Katze ist süß.

cards.title: All the possessives in one table
cards.body: Nine owners. One pattern. Masculine and neuter: no ending. Feminine and plural: -e. Learn the nine stems and use the ein-endings you already know.
cards.more: This is your cheat sheet. Step 1: find the owner row. Step 2: find the gender column. Step 3: read the word. For plural, use the column of feminine. Notice: mein, dein, sein, ihr, Ihr have an e added for feminine and plural. unser and euer too, but euer loses its middle e: eure. Extra example: Meine Tasche ist hier.

cards.title: The accusative with all of them
cards.body: The same rule as before. Only the masculine object changes: add -en. meinen, deinen, seinen, ihren, unseren, euren, Ihren. Everything else stays.
cards.more: This is the last step. You already know: only the masculine object adds -en. Step 1: is the noun masculine? Step 2: is it the object? Step 3: both yes? Add -en to the possessive: seinen, ihren, unseren. Step 4: everything else: nothing changes. Extra example: Ich sehe euren Hund.

lessons.title: können and the verb bracket
lessons.goal: Say what you can do and ask others, with the modal verb können.

grammar.point: A modal verb (können) is part 2. The other verb is an infinitive and goes to the end: Ich kann Tennis spielen.
grammar.oneLine: Ich kann Tennis spielen. Kannst du Gitarre spielen? Ich kann nicht schwimmen.

mistake.why: After kann, the second verb is the infinitive (spielen) and it goes to the end.

terms.meaning: a helper verb: können, müssen, wollen. It says can, must or want
two verbs that hold the sentence together: the modal in part 2 and the infinitive at the end
the basic form of a verb: spielen, kochen

cards.title: Before we start: can and the verb bracket
cards.body: Can you play the guitar? Can you come on Monday? To say what you can do, German uses a helper verb, and the sentence gets a new shape. The verb stays in part 2, but a second verb now waits at the very end.
steps: You already know: the verb is part 2 (Ich spiele Tennis, chapter 1)
New today: kann + a second verb at the end, a bracket around the sentence
By the end you can: say and ask what you can do, like Kannst du Gitarre spielen?

examples.why: New today: kann is part 2, spielen jumps to the end.
New today: the same bracket in a W-question.

cards.more: Picture a sentence as a parcel with two handles. The helper verb, here kann, holds the first handle in chair 2, exactly where your verb always sits. The other verb holds the last handle at the end of the sentence. Everything else, like the time and the thing, sits safely inside the parcel. Your chair 2 rule did not break, it just got a partner. You will learn it step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: können: can, to be able to
cards.body: können is a modal verb: a helper verb for can, must and want. Its forms are irregular. ich kann and er/sie kann have no ending. wir, sie and Sie can: können. Learn all six forms.
cards.more: Think of können as a tool that says what you are able to do. It has an odd shape: ich and er share the same short form, kann. Step 1: ich kann. Step 2: du kannst, with -st. Step 3: er, sie, es: kann again. Step 4: wir, sie, Sie: können. Step 5: ihr: könnt. Learn the table by heart. Extra example: Anna kann singen.

cards.title: The bracket: modal verb + infinitive at the end
cards.body: A modal verb is part 2 of the sentence. The second verb stays as an infinitive (spielen) and goes to the very end. The sentence is like a bracket: kann … spielen. Ich kann Tennis spielen.
cards.more: Imagine a bracket: ( kann ... spielen ). The first verb opens the bracket in chair 2. The second verb closes it at the very end. Everything else sits between the two verbs. Step 1: put the modal in part 2. Step 2: put the other things (object, time) in the middle. Step 3: close with the infinitive, unchanged. Extra example: Ich kann Suppe kochen.

cards.title: The middle: time, object and place
cards.body: Everything else goes in the middle, between the two verbs. The time can also lead the sentence: Am Montag kann ich Deutsch lernen. The modal is still part 2 and the infinitive is still at the end.

examples.de: Ich kann am Montag Deutsch lernen.
examples.en: I can learn German on Monday.

examples.de: Am Montag kann ich Deutsch lernen.
examples.en: On Monday I can learn German.
examples.why: time in chair 1: the modal is still part 2.

examples.de: Um acht Uhr können wir Kaffee trinken.
examples.en: At eight we can drink coffee.

cards.more: The bracket never breaks, no matter what goes inside. Step 1: first part of the sentence: the subject or a time word. Step 2: the modal in chair 2. Step 3: everything else in the middle. Step 4: the infinitive at the end. When the time goes first, the subject moves behind the modal, just like you learned in chapters 2 and 3. Extra example: Am Abend kann ich Suppe kochen.

cards.title: Ask: Kannst du …?
cards.body: A yes/no question starts with the modal. The infinitive is still at the end. Kannst du Gitarre spielen? Können Sie Deutsch sprechen? Kannst du …? is also a polite request.
cards.more: In a yes/no question the verb comes first. With a modal, that is the modal. The infinitive does not move: it still waits at the end. Step 1: Kannst. Step 2: du. Step 3: the rest. Step 4: the infinitive, with the question mark. Answer: Ja, ich kann Gitarre spielen. Or: Nein, ich kann nicht schwimmen. Extra example: Kannst du Klavier spielen?

cards.title: W-questions with können
cards.body: A W-question has the question word in chair 1, the modal in chair 2 and the infinitive at the end. Was kannst du gut? Wann kannst du kommen? Wo kann ich Kaffee kaufen?
steps: Was
Was kannst
Was kannst du
Was kannst du gut kochen?
cards.more: W-questions always follow the same recipe: question word, then the verb. If the verb is a modal, the other verb goes to the end. Step 1: question word in chair 1. Step 2: modal in chair 2. Step 3: subject. Step 4: rest of the sentence and infinitive at the end. Extra example: Wo kann ich Tee trinken?

cards.title: How well? gut, ein bisschen, nicht
cards.body: Say how well you can do something. gut = well. ein bisschen = a little. nicht = not. nicht goes before the infinitive: Ich kann nicht schwimmen. gut and ein bisschen stand before the infinitive too.

lessons.title: müssen and wollen: must and want
lessons.goal: Say what you must and want to do, and ask others.

grammar.point: müssen (muss, musst, müssen, müsst) and wollen (will, willst, wollen, wollt) work like können: the modal is part 2, the infinitive goes to the end.
grammar.oneLine: Ich muss am Montag arbeiten. Wir wollen Pizza essen. Ich muss nicht arbeiten.

mistake.why: After a modal, the other verb is the infinitive, with -en, at the end.

terms.meaning: a helper verb: können, müssen, wollen
something you have to do: müssen
something you want to do: wollen

cards.title: Before we start: must and want
cards.body: I must work on Monday. We want to eat pizza. Some things are duties and some are wishes. Today you learn two more helper verbs, müssen and wollen, and they work like the kann sentence from last lesson.
steps: You already know: kann in part 2 and the second verb at the end (the last lesson)
New today: müssen (must) and wollen (want to) in the same bracket
By the end you can: say what you must do and what you want to do

examples.why: New today: muss, the same shape as kann.
New today: wollen, the same shape again.

cards.more: Think of a toolbox with three helper tools: können for what you are able to do, müssen for what you have to do and wollen for what you want to do. All three fit into the same bracket, so the sentence builds the same way every time. Only the meaning changes. The new work is just their forms, for example ich muss and ich will, and one small trap with nicht. The next cards give you each tool, one at a time.

cards.title: müssen: must, have to
cards.body: müssen means must or have to. It says that you have no choice. The forms follow the same pattern as können: ich muss and er/sie muss have no ending. wir and sie/Sie: müssen. ihr: müsst.
cards.more: müssen is what your calendar says: things you cannot skip, like work, school or the dentist. Step 1: ich muss, no ending. Step 2: du musst, with -st. Step 3: er, sie, es: muss, like ich. Step 4: wir, sie, Sie: müssen. Step 5: ihr: müsst. Spot the pattern: it is the same shape as kann, kannst, können, könnt. Extra example: Anna muss arbeiten.

cards.title: müssen in the bracket: duties
cards.body: The bracket is the same as with können. müssen is part 2. The other verb goes to the end as an infinitive. Time and object stay in the middle. Ich muss am Montag um acht Uhr arbeiten.

examples.de: Ich muss am Montag um acht Uhr arbeiten.
examples.en: I have to work on Monday at eight.

examples.de: Am Montag muss ich um acht Uhr arbeiten.
examples.en: On Monday I have to work at eight.
Today we have to learn German.
examples.why: object and time in the middle.

cards.more: Same bracket, new verb. Step 1: modal in chair 2: muss. Step 2: put everything else between the two verbs: time, object. Step 3: the infinitive at the very end. Step 4: if the time goes first, the subject jumps behind the modal. The bracket is the same shape every time, so you only need to learn it once. Extra example: Heute muss ich Suppe kochen.

cards.title: wollen: to want to
cards.body: wollen means to want to. It is a modal verb too. ich will and er/sie will have no ending. du willst. wir, sie, Sie: wollen. ihr: wollt. The o becomes i for ich, du and er/sie.
cards.more: wollen is the verb of plans and wishes. Step 1: ich will, with the vowel i. Step 2: du willst. Step 3: er, sie, es: will. Step 4: wir, sie, Sie: wollen, with o again. Step 5: ihr: wollt. The pattern is the same as können and müssen: ich and er match, wir and sie match. Only the vowel is different. Extra example: Mira will Gitarre spielen.

cards.title: wollen or möchten?
cards.body: Both say what you want. ich will is strong and direct. ich möchte is polite. In a café, use möchte. Among friends, will is fine. both can take an infinitive: Ich will Kaffee trinken. Ich möchte Kaffee trinken.

examples.en: We want to eat pizza today.
examples.why: time and object in the middle.

cards.more: In English: I want a coffee can sound rude, but I would like a coffee sounds nice. German has the same two levels. möchten is the nice one: use it with waiters and strangers. wollen is plain: friends and plans. Step 1: ordering? möchten. Step 2: planning with friends? wollen. Step 3: with wollen, add the second verb at the end. Extra example: Ich will schwimmen.

cards.title: Ask and say no: Musst du …? nicht müssen
cards.body: Questions: modal first. Musst du heute arbeiten? Willst du Pizza essen? W-questions: Was willst du machen? Careful: ich muss nicht arbeiten means I do not have to work. nicht goes before the infinitive.

examples.en: Do you have to work today?

cards.more: Same recipes as before. Yes/no: modal first. W-question: question word, then modal. nicht comes before the infinitive. Be careful with meaning: Ich muss nicht arbeiten means I do not have to, so it is a free day, not forbidden. Step 1: pick the modal. Step 2: add nicht before the infinitive for no. Extra example: Wir müssen nicht warten.

cards.title: Three modals together: choose the right one
cards.body: können = can (I am able). müssen = must (I have to). wollen = want (I plan to). The sentence shape is identical. Only the meaning changes: Ich kann/muss/will heute arbeiten.
cards.more: Think of a sentence as a train with three possible engines: kann, muss, will. The cars behind it always stay the same: the time, the object, and the infinitive at the end. Step 1: choose the engine by meaning. Step 2: fit the ending to the person. Step 3: finish with the infinitive. Extra example: Wir wollen heute warten.

lessons.title: Make an appointment: phone calls and being late
lessons.goal: Book an appointment by phone, say yes or no, and say sorry for being late.

grammar.point: Use the modal bracket to propose and refuse a time: Können Sie am Dienstag kommen? Leider kann ich nicht kommen. Learn the phone pieces whole.
grammar.oneLine: Hier ist Leon. Ich möchte einen Termin. Haben Sie am Dienstag Zeit? Leider kann ich nicht kommen.

mistake.why: kommen is the infinitive after a modal, so it goes to the end.

terms.meaning: a fixed time to meet someone, for example at the doctor: der Termin
on time
a group of words you learn as one piece

cards.title: Before we start: making an appointment
cards.body: You call a doctor, a teacher or a friend and you want a time. You say who you are, what you want and when you can come. Today everything from this chapter works together in a phone call.
steps: You already know: Ich möchte einen Kaffee (chapter 4) and um + the time (this chapter)
New today: phone phrases, a short call, and how to say sorry when you are late
By the end you can: ask for an appointment and say yes, no or Es tut mir leid

examples.why: New today: the same sentence, a new thing, Termin.

examples.en: Do you have time on Tuesday?
examples.why: New today: a polite question with a day, to suggest a time.

cards.more: A phone call is a little story with a start, a middle and an end. First you say hello and who you are. Then you say what you want. Then you agree on a day and a time, and you say goodbye. You do not need new grammar for this. You use what you built in this chapter: möchte, am and um, and the bracket with kann. In the next cards you learn the small phrases that make the story sound polite and natural.

cards.title: A phone call: who you are, what you want
cards.body: On the phone, say who you are: Hier ist Leon. Then say what you want. Ich möchte einen Termin. Termin means appointment. Say bitte to be polite. Start with Guten Tag.

examples.why: hier ist = this is (on the phone).

examples.en: I would like an appointment, please.

steps: Guten Tag, Frau Weber.
Hier ist Leon.

cards.more: A phone call has a few fixed steps, like a little script. Step 1: greet: Guten Tag. Step 2: say who you are: Hier ist Leon. You say hier, here, because you are speaking from here. Step 3: say what you want with möchten: Ich möchte einen Termin. Step 4: add bitte. Learn Hier ist … as one piece. Extra example: Guten Morgen, hier ist Mira.

cards.title: Suggest a time: Haben Sie … Zeit? Können Sie …?
cards.body: To suggest a time, ask Haben Sie am Dienstag um zehn Uhr Zeit? Or use the bracket: Können Sie am Dienstag kommen? Say the day with am and the time with um.

examples.de: Haben Sie am Dienstag um zehn Uhr Zeit?
examples.en: Do you have time on Tuesday at ten?

examples.en: Can you come on Tuesday at half past two?

rows: Ja, ich habe am Montag Zeit.
Können Sie um zehn Uhr kommen?

cards.more: Two ways, one goal: find a time that fits. Way 1: Haben Sie Zeit? asks if the other person is free. Way 2: Können Sie kommen? asks if they can come. Both are yes/no questions, so the verb is first. With können, the other verb goes to the end. Step 1: the day with am. Step 2: the time with um. Step 3: the question. Extra example: Haben Sie am Montag Zeit?

cards.title: Say yes or no: Das passt gut. Leider …
cards.body: Yes: Das passt gut. (That suits me well.) No: Das passt nicht. Or say sorry: Leider kann ich am Montag nicht kommen. leider = unfortunately. Give a reason with müssen: Ich muss arbeiten.

examples.why: passen = to suit; learn Das passt gut as one piece.

examples.de: Leider kann ich am Montag nicht kommen.
examples.en: Unfortunately I cannot come on Monday.
examples.why: leider in chair 1: the modal is part 2.

examples.en: On Monday I have to work.

cards.more: To say no politely, do three things. Step 1: say leider, which means unfortunately. Step 2: say what you cannot do: kann ich nicht kommen. Step 3: give a short reason: Ich muss arbeiten. Then suggest another time. leider sits in chair 1, and the verb stays second, so the subject ich moves behind it. Extra example: Leider muss ich am Montag arbeiten.

cards.title: Confirm and say goodbye
cards.body: Repeat the time to be sure: Also, am Dienstag um halb drei. Say danke. On the phone, goodbye is Auf Wiederhören! Say Bis Dienstag! to say see you on Tuesday. Bis dann! means see you then.

examples.de: Also, am Dienstag um halb drei.
examples.en: So, on Tuesday at half past two.

examples.why: bis + day = see you on that day.

rows: Also, am Dienstag um halb drei.

cards.more: A call ends in three small steps, so nobody is confused. Step 1: repeat the day and time: Also, am Dienstag um halb drei. Step 2: thank: Danke. Step 3: say goodbye. Face to face you say Auf Wiedersehen, on the phone Auf Wiederhören. Hören is to hear, since you only hear the person. Extra example: Bis dann!

cards.title: Sorry I am late: Es tut mir leid
cards.body: Say sorry: Entschuldigung! or Es tut mir leid. Learn Es tut mir leid as one piece. To say you are late: Ich komme zu spät. Ich bin zu spät. Say how soon you arrive: Ich bin gleich da.

examples.why: learn zu spät as one piece.

examples.de: Es tut mir leid, ich bin zu spät.
examples.en: I am sorry, I am late.
I will be there in a moment.

rows: I will be there in a moment.

cards.more: Being late happens to everyone. What matters is what you say. Step 1: say sorry: Entschuldigung or Es tut mir leid. Step 2: say what is wrong: Ich komme zu spät. Step 3: say when you will arrive: Ich bin gleich da. Learn Es tut mir leid as one single piece, we explain why later. If the other person says Kein Problem!, it means no problem. Extra example: Der Bus ist zu spät.

cards.title: The sound r
cards.body: German has two r sounds. At the start of a word or before a vowel (rot, Reise, Frau), the r comes from the back of the throat, a soft gargle. At the end of a word (Vater, Uhr, Lehrer), r is like a soft a. Both are gentle.

examples.why: Vater: the -er at the end sounds like a soft a.
Frau and Lehrerin: r before a vowel.
vier and Uhr: r at the end.

cards.more: Do not roll the r like in Spanish. Make it soft, at the back of the throat, like a gentle gargle. Step 1: r at the start or before a vowel: rot, Reise, Frau. Step 2: r at the end of a word: very soft, almost like a. Step 3: -er at the end: Vater, Bruder, Lehrer sound like Vata, Bruda, Lehra. Step 4: practise by saying: Ruder, Bruder, Vater, Mutter. Extra example: Er arbeitet bis vier Uhr.

cards.title: Culture: being on time
cards.body: In Germany, pünktlich (on time) shows respect. For a doctor or an office, arrive 5 minutes early, not late. For a private visit, up to 10 minutes late is fine, but call and say it. If you are late, say sorry and tell them.

examples.de: Der Termin ist um zehn Uhr.
examples.en: The appointment is at ten o'clock.

examples.why: Trains: pünktlich is a big word.

rows: up to 10 minutes late is OK; say it
call and say Es tut mir leid

cards.more: In many countries, a few minutes late is normal. In Germany, a start time is a start time. Step 1: for a job, a doctor or a lesson, arrive a little before. Step 2: for a party with friends, a few minutes late is OK. Step 3: if you will be late, call: Es tut mir leid, ich komme zu spät. Step 4: being on time is a sign of respect, not stress. Extra example: Der Kurs beginnt um neun Uhr.
